doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

chapter: Swing Street shows and the business
title: The economics of making and selling your own CDs
summary: He works out the cost of producing a CD and the sales he expects at concerts.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: When you go to the jazz parties these days, there’s so much product out there, the CDs and so forth. I’m wondering, it must be hard to sell enough to really get any return on it.

Yeah. If you’re going to produce them yourself, actually you can produce them pretty inexpensively. I mean let’s face it. I mean if you do, even by musician’s scale, if you say for 20 minutes of recorded time you need a three hour session, for about a thousand dollars a player you can turn out a CD unless you really want to nit pick and really have

absolute perfection and arrangements. But if you’re doing the kind of music I like it’s pretty free-wheeling and if you’ve got a tape you just roll, you go on to the next tune and you roll. If there’s a clinker in there, so what? It’s jazz. So therefore, as a leader, with five guys it costs you $5,000 for the musicians. You’ve probably done the session in six hours, so that’s six hours of studio time at $75 an hour, that’s $450 of studio time. The mixing maybe another 4 hours, 5 hours. Cassettes, I mean CDs cost you about a dollar apiece for the CD, with the case and with the artwork, it should not have to cost you more than about $2.00 a CD. So once you’ve absorbed the thousand, let’s say $2,000 of studio time and musicians, if you buy a thousand CDs, the CDs are going to cost you $2.00 apiece and you’re going to have $3.00 apiece is going to be your cost, so your first thousand, the cost of your CDs is about $5 apiece, and you sell them for $15 or $20. It’s the only way to do it. But you need an outlet. And yes, at the jazz festivals you’re competing with so many of the other players at jazz parties, there’s so many CDs out there you’re not going to do it. But if you’ve got any number of concert gigs you can — so you sell a thousand a year, that’s 15 grand, right? And that’s only a thousand a year. But another thing, and I’ve compared my notes with other players is that if you see an audience of people who really are liking what you’re doing, if there’s a thousand people in the audience you will average a thousand dollars in sales for that concert, as long as it’s your CD that’s out there. So what you’re saying is a little under ten percent of the people will buy a CD. And it averages out. Every once in a while you’ll get double that and other ones you’ll merely bomb out. So having those concerts for Columbia Artists, financially it was great with the CDs.
